title: Acute encephalitis syndrome in children (India)
specialty: Paediatrics / Paediatric Neurology / Infectious Diseases / Critical Care

evidenceAudit.scope: Children with acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) in India: definition, stabilisation, seizure and raised intracranial pressure (ICP) control, empiric ceftriaxone, acyclovir and artesunate, investigations and referral, built on the ICMR STW for AES in Children (October 2019). Adult JE/AES is covered in the Japanese encephalitis topic.
findings: Definition, red flags, lumbar puncture contraindications, intubation criteria, 20 mL/kg fluid bolus, first- and second-line seizure drugs with doses, refractory status options, mannitol and 3% saline doses, PaCO2 and sodium targets, empiric ceftriaxone, acyclovir by age with stopping rules, artesunate dosing, investigations, supportive care and discharge criteria checked against the ICMR AES STW (October 2019).
Not clinically reviewed.
unverifiedSections: Scrub typhus is a major cause of AES in India but is not in the ICMR AES workflow; doxycycline or azithromycin are not dosed here (see Scrub typhus topic).
Phenytoin, valproate and levetiracetam as alternatives are listed without ranking when no ICU is available; the first-listed is marked preferred.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Acute encephalitis syndrome is acute fever (up to 5–7 days) with altered sensorium and/or new-onset seizures, excluding simple febrile seizures (ICMR STW). In India the main causes are Japanese encephalitis, scrub typhus, dengue, cerebral malaria, herpes simplex virus (HSV), bacterial meningitis and tuberculosis, with autoimmune encephalitis increasingly recognised. Brain inflammation and oedema raise intracranial pressure, and seizures and shock add secondary injury. Outcome depends on rapid stabilisation, seizure and ICP control, and early empiric treatment of the treatable causes (bacterial meningitis, HSV and malaria) while tests are pending.
keyMechanisms: Viral, bacterial or parasitic invasion inflames the brain parenchyma and meninges.
Cerebral oedema raises intracranial pressure and risks herniation.
Seizures increase cerebral metabolic demand and worsen injury.
Shock, hypoxia and hypoglycaemia cause secondary brain injury.

physicalSigns: Rash or eschar (scrub typhus), pallor, splenomegaly (malaria)
redFlags: GCS below 8 (ICMR STW)
Abnormal breathing pattern (ICMR STW)
Shock not responding to fluid bolus (ICMR STW)
Decerebrate or decorticate posturing (ICMR STW)
Seizures persisting despite benzodiazepine and phenytoin (ICMR STW)
precipitants: Endemic areas (eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Assam)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Brief generalised seizure, rapid full recovery; excluded from AES (ICMR STW).
CSF neutrophils, low glucose, positive culture.
Positive smear or RDT.
Hypoglycaemia, electrolyte disorder, poisoning history.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Acute onset fever (5–7 days or less) with altered sensorium and/or new-onset seizures, excluding simple febrile seizures.
GCS below 8, impaired airway reflexes, abnormal respiration, raised ICP, SpO2 below 92% despite high-flow oxygen, or fluid-refractory shock.
Papilloedema, platelets below 50,000, focal deficits, asymmetric or unreactive pupils, posturing: image first.

clinicalManagement.title: Stabilise
actions: Airway, breathing, circulation; intubate per criteria (ICMR STW).
Normal saline 20 mL/kg for circulatory failure; inotropes if needed (ICMR STW).
Maintain euglycaemia; treat fever (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Control seizures
actions: Benzodiazepine, then phenytoin (see medicines) (ICMR STW).
Refractory: PICU for midazolam infusion 1–18 mcg/kg/min; if no intensive care unit (ICU), valproate, levetiracetam or phenobarbitone (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat raised ICP
actions: Head end up 15–30°; sedation; avoid noxious stimuli (ICMR STW).
Mannitol or 3% saline (target sodium 145–155 mEq/L) (ICMR STW).
Impending herniation: hyperventilate to PaCO2 30–35 mmHg (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Empiric treatment
actions: Ceftriaxone, acyclovir and artesunate if CSF delayed and child unwell (ICMR STW).
Stop acyclovir if HSV PCR negative twice 24–48 hours apart and MRI not suggestive (ICMR STW).
Suspected ADEM or autoimmune encephalitis: pulse methylprednisolone (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Supportive care and referral
actions: Admit all; refer to a PICU with ventilation if any red flag (ICMR STW).
Physiotherapy, posture change, eye care, early feeding (ICMR STW).

title: Dengue in children (India)
specialty: Paediatrics / Infectious Diseases / Paediatric Critical Care

evidenceAudit.scope: Dengue in children in India: case categories, warning signs, outpatient care, weight-based fluid resuscitation for warning signs and shock, haematocrit-guided decisions, blood product thresholds and discharge, built on the ICMR Dengue Fever STW (October 2019) with paracetamol dosing from the ICMR Fever in Children STW. The adult Dengue (India adaptation) topic covers adults.
findings: Case categories, warning signs, investigations, outpatient care (paracetamol, avoid NSAIDs, daily PCV and platelets), crystalloid bolus 20 mL/kg over 15 minutes in shock, 10 mL/kg/hour for warning signs, the stepwise taper (10, 7, 5, 3 mL/kg/hour) stopping at 48 hours, platelet transfusion below 10,000/cumm or with bleeding, red cell and FFP indications and discharge criteria checked against the ICMR Dengue STW (October 2019).
Paracetamol 15 mg/kg from the ICMR Fever in Children STW.
Not clinically reviewed.
unverifiedSections: The ICMR Dengue STW is not child-specific; the mL/kg regimens are used for children as written.
Paracetamol interval and daily maximum are not given in the ICMR workflows (usual practice 4–6-hourly, no more than 60 mg/kg/day).
The ICMR flowchart lists some rate ranges without clear sequence; the main sequence is shown.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Dengue is a mosquito-borne flavivirus infection with yearly epidemics across India. Most children have a febrile phase of 2–7 days with fever, myalgia, rash and headache. Around defervescence, a critical phase of increased capillary permeability can cause plasma leakage, rising haematocrit, pleural effusion, ascites and shock, sometimes with bleeding and organ involvement. Warning signs (abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, liver enlargement over 2 cm) identify children who need hospital care (ICMR STW). Careful, haematocrit-guided fluid therapy prevents both shock and fluid overload; platelet transfusion is rarely needed.
keyMechanisms: Viral infection and immune activation increase vascular permeability.
Plasma leakage causes haemoconcentration, effusions and hypovolaemic shock.
Thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy cause bleeding.
Reabsorption of leaked fluid in recovery risks fluid overload.

symptoms: Headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, arthralgia, rash (ICMR STW)
physicalSigns: Liver enlargement over 2 cm (warning sign) (ICMR STW)
Weak rapid pulse, pulse pressure under 20 mmHg, cold clammy skin (shock) (ICMR STW)

Shock: weak rapid pulse, narrow pulse pressure, hypotension (ICMR STW)
Severe bleeding (ICMR STW)
Respiratory distress from fluid accumulation, impaired consciousness (ICMR STW)

clinicalManagement.title: Warning signs
actions: Ringer's lactate or normal saline 10 mL/kg/hour (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Shock
actions: Crystalloid or colloid 20 mL/kg over 15 minutes (ICMR STW).
Reassess HR, RR, BP, PCV hourly; if PCV rising give further fluid or colloid 10–20 mL/kg; if PCV falling with instability suspect bleeding and transfuse (ICMR STW).

Packed cells for overt blood loss of 10% or more of blood volume or refractory shock (ICMR STW).

actions: No fever for 48 hours, rising platelets, stable PCV without IV fluids, observed 24 hours after stopping fluids (ICMR STW).

pathophysiology.summary: Fever is the commonest reason children are brought to doctors in India. Most fevers are viral and self-limiting, but serious bacterial infections, malaria, dengue, enteric fever, scrub typhus, urinary infection and tuberculosis must not be missed. The ICMR approach is to assess how sick the child looks, look for a focus, treat danger signs at once, and use investigations only when they will change management: none for a well child with fever under 72 hours; blood count, smear and platelets after 72 hours; and a wider work-up for fever over 7 days (ICMR STW). Paracetamol treats discomfort; it does not treat the cause.
keyMechanisms: Pyrogenic cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF) reset the hypothalamic set point.
Infection is the usual trigger; inflammatory and malignant causes are less common.
Young infants have immature immunity and localise infection poorly.
Prolonged fever suggests TB, enteric fever, abscess, autoimmune disease or malignancy.

pathophysiology.summary: Status epilepticus is the commonest neurological emergency in children. A convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer is treated as SE, because seizures beyond 30 minutes are likely to cause lasting neuronal injury (ILAE, quoted by IAP). In Indian children, common causes are febrile seizures, neuroinfection (meningitis, encephalitis, neurocysticercosis), poor adherence in known epilepsy, metabolic derangements and trauma. Treatment is time-based: rescue benzodiazepine at home or at first contact, IV benzodiazepine at 5–20 minutes, a second-line drug at 20–40 minutes, and ICU-based anaesthetic infusions for refractory SE, while correcting hypoglycaemia and finding the cause.
keyMechanisms: Failure of seizure-termination mechanisms and excess excitation sustain seizures.
GABA-A receptors are internalised over time, so benzodiazepines work less well the longer SE lasts.
Prolonged seizures cause hypoxia, acidosis, hyperthermia and excitotoxic neuronal injury.
Underlying causes (infection, metabolic, structural) drive recurrence.

pathophysiology.summary: Acute asthma is a common cause of paediatric emergency visits in India, often triggered by viral infections, smoke from biomass fuels, dust and seasonal changes. Airway inflammation, bronchospasm and mucus narrow the airways, causing wheeze, breathlessness and hypoxaemia; a silent chest and exhaustion signal a life-threatening attack. Early inhaled salbutamol, ideally by metered-dose inhaler and spacer, and early oral steroid reduce admissions. Severe attacks need oxygen, nebulised salbutamol with ipratropium, and IV magnesium or other second-line drugs if there is no response (SIGN 158).
keyMechanisms: Allergen, viral or irritant triggers cause airway inflammation and smooth-muscle contraction.
Narrowed airways cause air trapping and ventilation-perfusion mismatch.
Fatigue and rising PaCO2 signal impending respiratory failure.
Beta-2 agonists relax airway smooth muscle; steroids reduce inflammation.

pathophysiology.summary: Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of preventable blindness in India, where diabetes is very common and often diagnosed late. Chronic hyperglycaemia damages retinal capillaries, causing microaneurysms, haemorrhages and leakage (non-proliferative DR), then capillary closure and ischaemia that drive new vessel growth (proliferative DR), with risk of vitreous haemorrhage and retinal detachment. Diabetic macular oedema can reduce vision at any stage. Vision is often normal until late, so every person with diabetes needs retinal screening at diagnosis and at least yearly (ICMR STW). Laser, intravitreal injections and vitreoretinal surgery at tertiary level prevent most severe vision loss if given in time.

Leaky capillaries and microaneurysms cause haemorrhages, exudates and macular oedema.
Capillary closure causes retinal ischaemia and VEGF release.
VEGF drives new fragile vessels that bleed and scar (proliferative DR).

pathophysiology.summary: Diabetic kidney disease develops in many people with long-standing type 2 diabetes and is a leading cause of kidney failure in India. Hyperglycaemia, glomerular hyperfiltration and hypertension damage the glomeruli, first causing albuminuria and later a falling eGFR. Because it is silent, everyone with diabetes needs yearly urine albumin-creatinine ratio (ACR) and creatinine (ICMR STW). Four treatments slow progression and reduce cardiovascular events: an ACE inhibitor or ARB at the highest tolerated dose when albuminuria is present, an SGLT2 inhibitor when eGFR is 20 or more, metformin adjusted to eGFR, and control of BP, lipids, smoking and salt (KDIGO 2022).
keyMechanisms: Hyperglycaemia and advanced glycation damage the glomerular basement membrane and podocytes.
Glomerular hyperfiltration raises intraglomerular pressure, causing albuminuria.
RAS blockade and SGLT2 inhibition lower intraglomerular pressure.
Progressive sclerosis lowers eGFR and leads to kidney failure.

pathophysiology.summary: Antepartum haemorrhage complicates 3–5% of pregnancies and is a leading cause of maternal and perinatal death (RCOG GTG 63). The important causes are placenta praevia (placenta in the lower segment, typically painless bright bleeding) and placental abruption (premature separation, typically painful with a tense uterus, and bleeding may be concealed). Severity is judged by blood loss and signs of shock, but visible loss underestimates abruption. Digital vaginal examination is avoided until praevia is excluded by ultrasound. Care focuses on resuscitation, assessing mother and fetus, steroids if preterm, anti-D if RhD-negative, and timely delivery.

Abruption: haemorrhage into the decidua separates the placenta, often with pain and uterine irritability.
Large abruption can cause disseminated intravascular coagulation and fetal hypoxia.
Hypovolaemia threatens maternal organs and placental perfusion.

title: Adult cardiac arrest: basic and advanced life support (India)

evidenceAudit.scope: In- and out-of-hospital adult cardiac arrest in India: high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), defibrillation, adrenaline and antiarrhythmics, reversible causes and post-resuscitation care, using the Resuscitation Council UK ALS algorithm (2025), the ERC 2021 ALS guideline (summary) and the AHA 2020 guideline, because no Indian national ALS guideline with doses could be opened.

Adrenaline 1 mg IV/IO, amiodarone 300 mg then 150 mg, lidocaine 100 mg then 50 mg, biphasic first shock at least 150 J, three stacked shocks for monitored arrest, thrombolysis with CPR for 60–90 minutes if PE suspected checked against the ERC 2021 summary.

pathophysiology.summary: Cardiac arrest is the sudden loss of effective cardiac output. In adults it is most often caused by coronary disease and ventricular fibrillation (VF) or pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pVT), but in Indian hospitals hypoxia, sepsis, haemorrhage, hyperkalaemia, poisoning and pulmonary embolism are common causes. Survival depends on the chain of survival: early recognition and call for help, immediate high-quality CPR, early defibrillation for shockable rhythms, adrenaline, treatment of reversible causes (4 Hs and 4 Ts) and structured post-resuscitation care.
keyMechanisms: VF or pVT: chaotic or very fast ventricular activity with no output; defibrillation restores organised rhythm.
PEA or asystole: usually from a reversible cause such as hypoxia, hypovolaemia or electrolyte disturbance.
Chest compressions generate coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure.
Adrenaline raises coronary perfusion through alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction.

title: Blood transfusion: indications, administration and reactions (India)
specialty: Transfusion Medicine / Haematology / Internal Medicine / Surgery

evidenceAudit.scope: Safe use of blood components in India: red cell, platelet, plasma and cryoprecipitate triggers and doses, administration, monitoring, and recognition, management and reporting of transfusion reactions under the Haemovigilance Programme of India (HvPI), built on the NIB Good Blood Transfusion Practices Guidance.
findings: Red cell thresholds (Hb 7 g/dL stable adults; 8 g/dL orthopaedic, cardiac surgery or cardiovascular disease; 7 g/dL non-bleeding obstetric), single-unit transfusion, FFP 10–15 mL/kg and INR above 1.5 rule, platelet dose (1 unit per 10 kg) and prophylactic and therapeutic triggers, cryoprecipitate indications, transport, sampling, cannula and filter, infusion rates and maximum times, monitoring schedule, reaction timeline and definitions, management steps and HvPI reporting checked against the NIB Good Blood Transfusion Practices Guidance.
Adrenaline dose for anaphylactic reactions from the WAO 2020 / RCUK 2021 sources used in the Anaphylaxis topic.
Not clinically reviewed.
unverifiedSections: The opened NIB text was truncated after the adrenaline dose; antipyretic and antihistamine doses are not given there.
Paediatric red cell volume is not in the opened text.
The adrenaline route in the NIB text was cut off; IM dosing is taken from the Anaphylaxis topic sources.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Blood components save lives but carry risks: wrong-blood errors, infection, reactions and fluid overload. Indian guidance favours restrictive red cell transfusion (Hb 7 g/dL in stable adults), single-unit transfusion with reassessment, and plasma and platelets only for defined indications (NIB). Most reactions happen early, so the first 15 minutes are given slowly with close observation. Any suspected reaction means stopping the transfusion, keeping the line open with saline, assessing airway, breathing and circulation, sending samples and the bag to the blood centre, and reporting to HvPI.
keyMechanisms: ABO-incompatible red cells cause intravascular haemolysis, shock and DIC.
Donor leucocyte or cytokine reactions cause febrile non-haemolytic reactions.
Plasma proteins trigger allergic and anaphylactic reactions.
Volume overload (TACO) and donor antibodies (TRALI) cause respiratory distress.

pathophysiology.summary: Seizures in newborns are often subtle — lip smacking, cycling movements, eye deviation, apnoea or heart-rate changes — and frequently reflect serious illness: hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, sepsis or meningitis, intracranial haemorrhage, or congenital infection. The ICMR workflow first secures temperature, airway, breathing and circulation, then corrects low glucose and calcium, then gives phenobarbitone and further drugs in sequence, while investigating the cause. Most babies need only short treatment; long-term neurodevelopmental and hearing follow-up is essential.
keyMechanisms: The immature brain is excitable because GABA can be excitatory in early life.
Hypoxia-ischaemia, hypoglycaemia and hypocalcaemia lower the seizure threshold.
Infection and haemorrhage injure the cortex directly.
Prolonged seizures worsen brain injury.

pathophysiology.summary: Psychosis is loss of contact with reality — hallucinations, delusions and disorganised behaviour — and schizophrenia is its commonest chronic form. In India most patients first present to families, faith healers or primary care. The ICMR workflow asks primary care to suspect psychosis (talking or laughing to self, suspiciousness, poor self-care, decline in function), exclude organic causes and substance use, assess risk to self and others, start risperidone with trihexyphenidyl if needed, and refer when diagnosis is unclear, risk is high, response is poor or special situations (pregnancy, comorbidity) exist. Treatment is long term; clozapine is used after two adequate failed trials.
keyMechanisms: Excess mesolimbic dopamine activity is linked to positive symptoms.
Antipsychotics block dopamine D2 receptors; blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway causes extrapyramidal symptoms.
Second-generation antipsychotics also block serotonin 5-HT2A and cause more metabolic effects.
Clozapine is effective in treatment resistance but causes neutropenia, myocarditis and seizures.

pathophysiology.summary: Anxiety disorders are the commonest mental disorders and often present in Indian primary care as physical complaints — palpitations, breathlessness, headache, abdominal symptoms — with repeated investigations. The ICMR workflow asks clinicians to identify the type of disorder, assess duration and impairment, look for depression, substance use and physical causes (thyrotoxicosis, phaeochromocytoma, hypoglycaemia), give psychoeducation and start escitalopram. Benzodiazepines are only for short-term relief of severe anxiety. Non-responders move to a second SSRI and CBT at district level, and to tertiary care after that.
keyMechanisms: Over-activity of fear circuits (amygdala) with reduced prefrontal control.
Serotonin and noradrenaline systems modulate anxiety; SSRIs reduce symptoms over weeks.
Avoidance maintains anxiety by preventing new learning.
OCD involves cortico-striatal circuits; responds to SSRIs and exposure-based CBT.

Not clinically reviewed.

pathophysiology.summary: Burns are a major cause of injury in India, especially among women (kitchen and kerosene fires) and children (scalds). Early care decides survival: stop the burning process, cool the wound with running water, assess the airway for inhalation injury, estimate TBSA and depth, start Ringer lactate by formula for large burns, and titrate to urine output rather than the formula alone. Pain relief should be intravenous in the acute phase. Prophylactic antibiotics are not used. Patients meeting referral criteria — large or full-thickness burns, special areas, inhalation, electrical or chemical injury, extremes of age — go to a burns unit.
keyMechanisms: Heat causes coagulative necrosis surrounded by zones of stasis and hyperaemia; cooling limits progression.
Capillary leak in burns above about 15% TBSA causes hypovolaemic burn shock in the first 24 hours.
Smoke causes upper airway oedema, chemical pneumonitis, and carbon monoxide or cyanide poisoning.
Circumferential full-thickness eschar restricts breathing or limb circulation.

Keep the patient warm; cover with cling film or clean sheet (NZ NBS).

clinicalManagement.title: Primary survey
actions: Airway: early intubation for stridor, facial and neck burns or inhalation (DGHS STG).
Oxygen to SpO2 92–95%; high-flow oxygen 8–15 L/min for at least 6 hours if carbon monoxide suspected (DGHS STG).
Two large-bore IV lines; weigh the patient (DGHS STG).

clinicalManagement.title: Fluid resuscitation
actions: Adults above 15% TBSA: Ringer lactate 3 mL/kg/%TBSA (modified Parkland) or 2 mL/kg/%TBSA plus maintenance (modified Brooke); half in 8 hours, half in 16 hours (DGHS STG).
Children 10% or more: Ringer lactate 2 mL/kg/%TBSA plus maintenance (4-2-1 mL/kg/h) (DGHS STG).
Adults under 15%: oral fluids at least 2 L (DGHS STG).
Titrate to urine output; fluid challenge 250 mL if output 0.25–0.5 mL/kg/h (COBIS).

clinicalManagement.title: Pain, tetanus and wound
actions: IV opioid for severe pain; avoid IM injections in shock (DGHS STG).
Tetanus toxoid 0.5 mL IM if not already given (DGHS STG).
1% silver sulfadiazine or silver dressings; leave small blisters; no routine antibiotics (DGHS STG).
Escharotomy for circumferential full-thickness chest or limb burns (DGHS STG).

clinicalManagement.title: Refer
actions: Use DGHS referral criteria to secondary or tertiary burns care (DGHS STG).

title: Essential newborn thermal care and hypothermia (India)

evidenceAudit.scope: Warm chain and thermal care of newborns in Indian delivery rooms, postnatal wards and transport: drying, skin-to-skin contact, Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC), temperature measurement, grading and management of hypothermia and hyperthermia, with vitamin K prophylaxis at birth, built on the ICMR Thermal Care of Newborn STW (July 2020) and the NHM vitamin K guideline.
findings: Temperature thresholds (normal 36.5–37.5°C; mild 36.0–36.4; moderate 32–35.9; severe below 32; hyperthermia above 37.5), axillary digital measurement and frequency, delivery room above 25°C, warmer on 20–30 minutes before birth, prewarmed towels, immediate drying, skin-to-skin for 1 hour or until first breastfeed, warm chain in wards and transport, management by grade (radiant warmer servo mode, oxygen if SpO2 below 91%, glucose below 45 mg/dL, 15-minute rechecks, nil by mouth and IV fluids in severe) checked against the ICMR Thermal Care of Newborn STW (July 2020).
Vitamin K 1 mg IM (0.5 mg if under 1000 g) to all facility births checked against the NHM vitamin K guideline (reported 2017).
Dextrose 10% 2 mL/kg for glucose below 45 mg/dL from the ICMR Neonatal Seizures STW, matching the Neonatal Hypoglycaemia STW threshold.
Not clinically reviewed.
unverifiedSections: Rewarming rate is not given in the STW (only recheck intervals).
Cord care and bathing technique are not covered beyond delaying bathing.
The vitamin K guideline was read in a secondary news report of the NHM guideline.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Newborns lose heat quickly through a large surface area, wet skin and little fat, and hypothermia increases death and illness, especially in low birth weight and preterm babies. The warm chain — a warm delivery room, immediate drying, skin-to-skin contact, early breastfeeding, delayed bathing, rooming-in, KMC and warm transport — prevents most hypothermia. Temperature must be measured, not guessed. The ICMR workflow grades hypothermia and links each grade to action, from skin-to-skin contact for mild cold stress to radiant warmer, glucose check, IV fluids and vitamin K for severe hypothermia. All facility-born babies should receive vitamin K prophylaxis.
keyMechanisms: Heat loss by evaporation (wet skin), conduction, convection and radiation.
Newborns produce heat by non-shivering thermogenesis in brown fat, using oxygen and glucose.
Cold stress leads to hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, acidosis and poor feeding.
Hot trunk with cold extremities suggests sepsis rather than environmental heat.

clinicalManagement.title: Delivery room
actions: Room above 25°C; warmer on 20–30 minutes before; prewarm towels (ICMR STW).
Dry immediately; skin-to-skin for 1 hour or until first breastfeed; weigh after feeding (ICMR STW).
Vitamin K IM after skin-to-skin and breastfeeding start (NHM).

clinicalManagement.title: Postnatal ward and transport
actions: Rooming-in, cover the baby, avoid draughts and fans; KMC for eligible babies; delay bathing (ICMR STW).
Transport: skin-to-skin or thermal mattress or transport incubator; never a naked baby on a trolley (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Mild hypothermia (36.0–36.4°C)
actions: Room 25–28°C; skin-to-skin; continue breastfeeding (ICMR STW).
Still below 36.5°C at 1 hour: treat as moderate (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Moderate hypothermia (32–35.9°C)
actions: Radiant warmer in servo mode; oxygen if SpO2 below 91%; check glucose (ICMR STW).
Continue feeds if stable (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Severe hypothermia (below 32°C)
actions: Nil by mouth; IV fluids; vitamin K injection (ICMR STW).
Shock or respiratory failure: refer to higher centre (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Hyperthermia
actions: Cooler environment, fewer clothes, adequate breastfeeding, check weight (ICMR STW).
